newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers in McVeigh trial seek bond with jurors.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers in McVeigh trial seek bond with jurors.

text.p: If you want to meet friendly people at the Oklahoma City bombing trial, head straight for the prosecution table, where normally hard-nosed prosecutors are acting like they want to bond with every juror they question.
The friendliness, which legal experts call a classic courtroom technique, began almost the minute jury selection started on Monday.

One of the first potential jurors said she was a personal shopper who buys gifts for people too busy to shop themselves. A beaming prosecutor, Beth Wilkinson, asked if she could engage her services and federal Judge Richard Matsch had to intervene. "Not until after the trial," he cautioned.

A couple of days later prosecutor Patrick Ryan, the U.S. attorney for Oklahoma City, asked a newly married self-employed window washer if he had any children. When the man said no, just a dog, Ryan asked, "What kind?"
"A Labrador retriever," the man said. "Great dog," Ryan said, adding, "What colour, black?" "No," came the reply, "Chocolate." Ryan liked that colour as well.

After he finished questioning another prospect, an elderly lady who once was a jury forewoman, Ryan told her, "You are a remarkable person and we are delighted to have you here today." Unlike many other people questioned, the woman appeared quite willing to serve.

Experts say the legal lions are deliberately acting like friendly lambs; the charm offensive is designed to make a good first impression in a case where the defence might try to put the government on trial in its bid to save Timothy McVeigh.

McVeigh is accused of planting the bomb that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people and injuring 500 others. The defence says the government has the wrong man and plans to attack its evidence against him as tainted.

Almost every witness who gets on the stand is greeted with a big smile by a prosecutor, who wants to know where he or she came from, what sports they like, what books they have read. A nurse was asked if she watched the hit TV series "ER" and whether it was realistic. She assured them it was not.
When the woman said she was about to go on vacation, prosecutor Lawrence Mackey told her, "Enjoy your trip."

The defence, while not discourteous, has often had to play the tough guys, especially with those who think McVeigh is guilty. Chief defence lawyer Stephen Jones often tells jurors who have been less than forthcoming that the trial will last months and hear 500 witnesses.

McVeigh, a tall bony man of 28, frequently flashes a boyish grin at potential jurors and laughs loudly at the courtroom jokes. He has taken to rising and bowing when jurors are brought into court and introduced to the defence table.
Denver lawyer Andrew Cohen, a legal consultant to CBS and the Denver Post, said the prosecution's charm offensive was deliberate.

"They are making a conscious effort to be friendly and charming to the jurors because they know you don't get a second chance to make a first impression. If the potential juror is chosen for the jury, he will remember how nicely he was treated. I am surprised that the defence is not doing the same thing. Their tone is stern."
